title: "Report.txt" and "report.txt" are the same file on a default Mac or Windows disk, but "==" says no
assumption: If two path strings compare unequal, they refer to different files.

input.description: A second upload, a cache key, or a git checkout where only the case of a filename differs from an existing one.

what_goes_wrong: A uniqueness check (a set of seen paths, a dict key, a plain == comparison) treats the two strings as different files, while the OS silently aliases the second "create" onto the first, or vice versa.
why: macOS's default APFS volume format is case-insensitive but case-preserving: it keeps the case you typed but treats names differing only in case as the same entry (a case-sensitive APFS variant exists but is not the default). Windows treats names case-insensitively by default too, though NTFS directories can be flagged case-sensitive individually; Linux ext4 is case-sensitive. Pure path libraries never consult the disk: PurePosixPath and Node's path.posix compare the literal strings, so a case difference always compares unequal. (pathlib.PureWindowsPath, by contrast, compares case-insensitively, so pathlib's answer depends on which flavour you picked, not on the disk underneath.)
affects: windows ntfs (case-insensitive by default; per-directory case sensitivity can be enabled)

repros.code:
from pathlib import PurePosixPath
a = PurePosixPath("/Users/me/Report.txt")
b = PurePosixPath("/Users/me/report.txt")
print(a == b, str(a) == str(b))

repros.note: On a default (case-insensitive) APFS volume, opening /Users/me/report.txt for writing when /Users/me/Report.txt already exists opens the existing file; the directory keeps one entry, still spelled Report.txt.

fix: Decide your own case policy at the application layer (usually: normalize to one case before using a path as a key) rather than trusting string equality or the filesystem's default behavior, since the two disagree and the filesystem's own behavior varies by volume format.

sources.title: Apple File System Guide: FAQ (case sensitivity)
Microsoft Learn: Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces

test_cases.note: A filename-key function meant to be safe on default macOS and Windows disks should map these to the same key, because those disks treat them as one file.
